steps.en: What you see: The mid interatrial septum drops out on subcostal views with left to right colour flow across it. The right atrium and right ventricle dilate from chronic volume overload while the left heart stays normal in size. The pulmonary trunk looks dilated relative to the aorta. Secundum defects of the fossa ovalis are the commonest type, with sinus venosus, primum and coronary sinus types each needing their own views.

Normal values with units: Defect diameter. Small below 10 mm. Moderate 10 to 20 mm. Large above 20 mm with right heart enlargement.. Source: ASE and SCA 2013 transoesophageal examination guideline, section on atrial septal assessment

Pulmonary to systemic flow ratio. Below 1.5 small. From 1.5 to 2.0 moderate. Above 2.0 large. Closure is considered at 1.5 or above with right heart enlargement.. Source: ASE 2019 transthoracic examination guideline, section on Doppler and haemodynamics

Device closure rims. Rims of 5 mm or more around the defect generally suit device closure, assessed best on transoesophageal imaging.. Source: ASE and SCA 2013 transoesophageal examination guideline, section on atrial septal assessment

Right ventricular basal diameter. Normal 41 mm or below in the focused view. Volume overload dilates it beyond this with a flattened septum in diastole.. Source: ASE 2019 transthoracic examination guideline, section on the right ventricle

ECG and heart sound correlation ecg: Right bundle branch block with an rSR pattern in lead V1 is the classic signature. Right axis deviation with right ventricular hypertrophy follows large shunts. Atrial arrhythmia appears once the right atrium enlarges.

ECG and heart sound correlation sounds: A wide fixed split second sound never varies with breathing. An ejection systolic murmur at the upper left sternal edge marks high pulmonary flow. A mid diastolic rumble at the lower left sternal edge marks a large shunt.

What to report: Defect type, position and diameters in two planes with the views used
Every rim measurement for the device closure decision
Flow ratio with the diameters and integrals stated, plus right heart sizes
Pulmonary pressure, shunt direction and any anomalous veins or valve cleft
Red flags needing urgent referral: Cyanosis with right to left flow, needs urgent review for pulmonary vascular disease
Paradoxical embolism with stroke in a young patient, needs urgent closure assessment
Heart failure in infancy with a large defect and pulmonary hypertension, needs urgent paediatric cardiology review
Pitfalls: Pulmonary vascular disease reverses the shunt and silences the murmur, so check direction before closure is ever discussed.
Primum defects travel with a cleft mitral valve, so grade the left atrioventricular valve in every primum case.
A patent foramen ovale is a flap, not a true defect, and needs bubble contrast with Valsalva to prove.

todo.en: How to get it on the probe, step by step: Start subcostal bicaval and sweep the septum from superior to inferior vena cava with colour on.
Measure the defect diameter in two planes at end systole when the hole looks largest.
Measure each rim: aortic, superior, inferior, posterior and atrioventricular valve rims.
Quantify pulmonary to systemic flow ratio from outflow diameters and velocity time integrals.
Check pulmonary veins, sinus venosus drainage and the atrioventricular valves for associated lesions.
Common mistakes and how to correct them: Calling dropout near the aortic root a defect. Fix: Drop colour gain until noise just clears and confirm the jet in two planes with the same direction.
Trusting a flow ratio from one off axis measurement. Fix: Angle the beam perpendicular to flow and average three beats. Small angle errors square in the flow ratio.
Missing a sinus venosus defect with anomalous vein drainage. Fix: Sweep superiorly to the cava junction and follow each pulmonary vein to the atrium.

remember.en: Recognise shunt reversal and anomalous drainage as referral red flags.

q.en: How does a secundum defect differ from a patent foramen ovale?

o.en: A true hole with left to right flow on colour at rest
A flap seen only with bubble contrast on Valsalva release
A muscular wall with no flow

why.en: A true defect shunts at rest on colour Doppler while the foramen flap opens only transiently with provocation.

o.en: 1.5 or above with right heart enlargement

why.en: A ratio of 1.5 or above with right heart enlargement marks a significant shunt worth closing.

q.en: What does the device closure assessment need?

o.en: Aortic, superior, inferior, posterior and atrioventricular valve rims

why.en: Rims of 5 mm or more around the defect anchor the device, so every rim is measured, best on transoesophageal imaging.

q.en: Flow turns right to left with cyanosis. What next?

o.en: Urgent review for pulmonary vascular disease, closure is off the table until assessed

why.en: Shunt reversal marks pulmonary vascular disease where closure would be fatal, so urgent specialist assessment comes first.

q.en: Which sound is classic for a large shunt?

o.en: Early diastolic murmur at the base

why.en: The split never varies with breathing because atrial pressures equalise across the defect.
